chapter.name: Earth, Moon, and the Sun
chapter.blurb: Rotation and revolution of the Earth, day and night, the night sky, seasons, and solar and lunar eclipses.

concepts.name: Rotation of the Earth, day and night
concepts.description: The merry-go-round activity, the Earth's rotation, its axis, and how it causes day and night and the Sun's apparent motion.
concepts.idea: The Earth rotates from West to East once in about 24 hours, causing day and night and the apparent motion of the Sun.
concepts.rule: On a merry-go-round turning anti-clockwise, objects around you seem to turn clockwise. Similarly the Sun seems to move from East to West because we view it from the Earth, which is turning. The Earth spins on its axis of rotation, an imaginary line passing through the geographic North Pole and South Pole, and completes one rotation in about 24 hours. Viewed from above the North Pole it rotates anti-clockwise, from West to East. Rotation is the motion of an object in which all parts move in circles around an imaginary line called the axis of rotation. With a globe and a torch, half of the globe is lit (day) and the other half dark (night). Light falls on eastern India first when the globe rotates from West to East, so sunrise is earlier in the east. The rotation causes the day-night cycle: sunrise as a place moves into light and sunset as it moves into darkness. The Sun appears to rise in the East, cross the sky and set in the West, then stars become visible.
concepts.example: Rashmika noticed shadows are longer in the morning than in the afternoon.

concepts.name: Apparent motion of stars, the Pole Star and ancient Indian astronomy
concepts.description: How the Earth's rotation makes stars appear to move, star trails, the Foucault pendulum and Aryabhata.
concepts.idea: The stars appear to move around the Pole Star because the Earth rotates.
concepts.rule: In Activity 12.3 the Big Dipper (Saptarishi) is sketched every two hours on the same night and appears to move around the Pole Star (Dhruva Tara). The Earth's axis of rotation points very close to the Pole Star in the Northern Hemisphere, so it appears nearly stationary and all other stars appear to move around it. Like the Sun, the Moon appears to rise in the East and set in the West. Long exposure photographs show star trails, arcs of circles. Leon Foucault used a long pendulum in the middle of the nineteenth century to give the first simple demonstration of the Earth's rotation, and a 22-metre Foucault pendulum hangs in the Constitution Hall of the new Parliament building. Aryabhata (fifth century CE), in the Aryabhatiya, explained the apparent motion of stars, likening it to a man in a boat who sees stationary objects moving backwards, and gave the Earth's rotation time as about 23 hours 56 minutes 4.1 seconds.
concepts.example: Star trails record the apparent motion of stars as arcs.

concepts.name: Revolution of the Earth and the changing night sky
concepts.description: Revolution, orbit, the year, and why different stars appear at different times of the year.
concepts.idea: The Earth revolves around the Sun in about 365 days and 6 hours, and the night sky changes through the year.
concepts.rule: Revolution is the motion of an object around another object, and the path taken is its orbit. Viewed from the top, the Earth's orbit around the Sun is nearly circular; it looks elongated only in side views. The Earth completes one revolution in about 365 days and 6 hours. As the Earth revolves, the stars seen in the night sky after sunset gradually change over a year because we look in different directions; different stars rise at sunset in different months. This can be noticed by looking at a star pattern at a fixed time on days a month apart. The Bhil and Pawara communities of the Tapi Valley used the appearance of certain star patterns as markers for the arrival of monsoon rain. Rotation and revolution are different motions.
concepts.example: The stars that rise at sunset change from month to month.

concepts.name: Seasons and the tilt of the Earth's axis
concepts.description: How the tilt and spherical shape of the Earth cause seasons, and common incorrect explanations.
concepts.idea: Seasons are caused by the tilt of the Earth's axis and its spherical shape.
concepts.rule: The Earth's axis of rotation is tilted with respect to its orbit, and the Earth keeps this tilt as it orbits the Sun. In June the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, so the same amount of sunrays is spread over a smaller area and heats more intensely, and daytime lasts more than 12 hours, causing summer. In December the Northern Hemisphere is tilted away, with less intense sunlight for a shorter time, causing winter. Seasons are reversed in the Southern Hemisphere: winter in June and summer in December. Two incorrect explanations are that the tilted hemisphere is closer to the Sun and that the oval orbit changes the distance greatly; in fact the Earth is closest to the Sun in January and the differences are very small. On the equator there are always 12 hours of daylight and little variation in intensity, so seasons are not very prominent in southern India.

concepts.name: Solstices, equinoxes and day length across the Earth
concepts.description: Summer and winter solstice, equinoxes, the poles and the equator.
concepts.idea: Day length changes with season, except at the equator, and the poles have six months of day and night.
concepts.rule: In the Northern Hemisphere the longest day occurs around 21 June, the summer solstice; after it days become shorter and nights longer. The shortest day and longest night occur around 22 December, the winter solstice. Around 21 March and 23 September, daytime lasts 12 hours; these are the spring and autumn equinoxes in the Northern Hemisphere. At the North Pole the Sun rises on the equinox 21 March and remains in the sky for six months, setting on 22 September; the South Pole experiences the opposite, so polar regions have six months of continuous sunshine followed by six months of darkness. On the equator there are always 12 hours of sunlight and 12 hours of darkness. In June the North Pole receives sunlight for all 24 hours, and in December it is in darkness for 24 hours. Local features and nearness to oceans also influence the seasons.
concepts.example: Chennai has little variation in day length because it is close to the equator.

concepts.name: Solar eclipse
concepts.description: Why the Moon can cover the Sun, total and partial solar eclipses, and safe viewing.
concepts.idea: A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth, blocking sunlight.
concepts.rule: At certain times the Moon comes in between the Sun and the Earth and obstructs the Sun's light, a solar eclipse. The Moon can cover the Sun because the apparent size depends on both physical size and distance: the Moon is much smaller than the Sun but much closer, so their apparent sizes are similar; Mercury and Venus are larger than the Moon but much farther, so they cannot block the Sun (Venus appears as a tiny dot in a rare Transit of Venus). The Moon's shadow falls on a small area of the Earth where a total solar eclipse is seen, and a partial solar eclipse elsewhere. During totality it turns dark for a few minutes as the Moon's shadow moves across the Earth. Never view a solar eclipse directly, even through sunglasses, binoculars or telescopes; use specialised eye protection at events by planetaria or astronomy clubs, or project the Sun's image with a mirror under a teacher's supervision. Eclipses are called grahan; the Surya Siddhanta gives calculations to predict them. Superstitions have no scientific basis.
concepts.example: The thumb can cover a friend's head when held close.

concepts.name: Lunar eclipse and Indian astronomy
concepts.description: The Earth's shadow on the Moon, viewing, Stellarium, Kodaikanal Observatory and Vainu Bappu.
concepts.idea: A lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon, and it can be watched safely.
concepts.rule: As the Moon revolves around the Earth, sometimes the Earth blocks sunlight from reaching the Moon: a lunar eclipse. We see the Earth's shadow fall on the full disc of the Moon. When the Moon is completely in the Earth's shadow it is a total lunar eclipse and the Moon appears dark red until it moves out; when part is in shadow it is a partial lunar eclipse. Unlike the Sun, an eclipsed full Moon can be seen safely with the naked eye. The order is Sun, Earth, Moon. Lunar eclipses are visible from a large part of the Earth while total solar eclipses are visible from a small part. The free Stellarium app gives information about upcoming eclipses. The Kodaikanal Solar Observatory, established in 1899 in the Palani hills, is operated by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics, Bengaluru. M.K. Vainu Bappu, the father of modern Indian astronomy, set up telescopes at Manora Peak and Kavalur, studied stars, discovered a comet and travelled to study solar eclipses.
concepts.example: The eclipsed Moon looks dark red.

questions.q: Compare why lunar eclipses are widely visible and total solar eclipses are not.
questions.a: The Earth's shadow is large and covers the whole Moon for all on the night side, whereas the Moon's shadow on the Earth is small.

questions.q: Why does the Moon look red during a total lunar eclipse instead of vanishing?
questions.a: some sunlight still reaches it bent through the Earth's air

questions.q: Compare a solar and a lunar eclipse in what blocks the light.
questions.a: In a solar eclipse the Moon blocks light to the Earth; in a lunar eclipse the Earth blocks light to the Moon.

questions.q: Why is it important to preserve observatories that gather Sun data over a century?
questions.a: Long records help track solar changes and support research and understanding of the Sun.

questions.q: 'A lunar eclipse happens when the Moon comes between the Sun and Earth.' Evaluate.
questions.a: False: that is a solar eclipse; in a lunar eclipse the Earth is between the Sun and Moon.

questions.q: Design a model with a torch, ball and globe to show a lunar eclipse.
questions.a: Use a torch as Sun, a globe as Earth and a small ball as Moon in the shadow, showing the shadow falling on the Moon.
